description: Nubel Team uses Earth observation, GIS, and open data to address environmental challenges. We are building a wildfire monitoring platform for Peru using NASA FIRMS, MODIS, and VIIRS data. Our skills include remote sensing, React, APIs, visualization, and UX. We welcome teammates interested in environmental science, GIS, Google Earth Engine, data science, machine learning, backend development, and scientific storytelling.
summary: We are a five-person team combining data science, web development and geospatial skills to tackle wildfires in Peru. Our project merges NASA FIRMS hotspot data from MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) into a single harmonized series, so a change of sensor isn’t mistaken for a change in fire activity. In our web app, firefighters, scientists and land managers pick a department and a date range. They then get a fire-activity calendar, compare each month with its historical median and download the data as CSV. Our goal is to turn decades of satellite observation into clear, actionable information for people on the ground.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Nikal turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections over Cusco, Peru, into one consistent historical series, and helps people see it, understand it and act on it.

The app is organized in three chapters plus a live mode:

  • Look: a map of hotspot density, a season ribbon at the bottom (year total, its rank among the 25 years, the "this year vs usual" curve and one bar per year from 2000 to 2025), a data panel with an exact date range, key metrics, a CSV download and a technical report, and a months × years calendar.
  • Understand: the season explained in plain words and simple charts.
  • Act: a hazard level by province, district or river basin, with an automated report for each unit.
  • Live: near-real-time FIRMS detections from the last 24 hours, 48 hours or 5 days, refreshed every 15 minutes and shown separately because they are not harmonized.

2020 selected. The map shows where hotspots concentrated, the ribbon says 2020 had 1,206 harmonized hotspots (#2 of 25 years, peak in August), and the panel offers the metrics, the calendar, the CSV and the technical report.

Link Github: https://github.com/Jyron1310/NASA_NUBEL_TEAM_NIKAL

What benefits does it have?

  • Honest comparison across 25 years. The 2012 sensor jump is removed, so a bad year really is a bad year.
  • Answers in plain words. The Understand chapter states how the current year compares with a typical one, when the season starts and peaks, and where most hotspots occur, without remote-sensing jargon.
  • Any two periods side by side. Compare splits the map in two so changes between years or seasons are visible at a glance.
  • Each place compared with itself. Anomalies are measured against the median of the same month in the same area, which is more useful to a local manager than a raw count.
  • Ready-to-use outputs. CSV downloads and automated HTML reports per province, district or basin, with the method and its limits.
  • Accessible. Bilingual (English and Spanish), works on a phone, uses accessible colors and needs no installation.
  • Guided from the first visit. A six-step tutorial walks new users through the study area, the Look / Understand / Act chapters, the data filters and downloads, the map tools, the season ribbon and the legend, so a municipal officer or brigade leader can use the app in under two minutes without GIS training. It can be reopened anytime from the ? button.

"In 2025, Cusco recorded 387 harmonized hotspots, 30% fewer than a typical year (555). The season runs from July to October and peaks in September." The gray band shows where 8 in 10 years fall

Guided tutorial, step 3 of 6: the tour highlights the Data filters panel and explains how to choose a period, review indicators and download the calendar, CSV or technical report.

What is the intended impact of the project?

To move fire management in Cusco from reacting to preparing, on a baseline that institutions can trust.

  • Before the season: the app shows that the season usually starts in July, so June is the month to get ready, and that half of all hotspots occur below 1,500 m. Brigades, awareness campaigns against agricultural burning and burn permits can be planned around those months and places.
  • Where to focus: the Act chapter ranks provinces, districts and basins in CENEPRED's four-level hazard format (very high, high, medium, low). In 2020, the 4 very-high provinces out of 13 held 74% of the hotspots, 80% of them between 13 July and 23 October.
  • Evidence for plans: each unit gets an automated report that a municipality or the regional government can attach to its prevention plan or to a CENEPRED risk assessment.
  • After the season: judge whether a year was truly anomalous and whether prevention worked.

Intended users: the Regional Government of Cusco, municipalities, CENEPRED, INDECI, SERFOR, fire brigades, rural communities and researchers. In the longer term, the same method can be applied to any region where fire must be compared before and after 2012.

"The season usually starts in July: June is the month to get ready", plus the share of hotspots by elevation band.

Hazard level by province in CENEPRED format. The map is painted by level and the panel summarizes when each level concentrates its hotspots.

Automated report for Anta province: very high hazard, rank 1 of 13, with its parameters and a plain-words summary.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS Terra and Aqua; VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20), annual country archives plus the Area API for the live layer, with the MAP_KEY kept in Google Secret Manager. FAO GAUL boundaries and NASA SRTM elevation via Google Earth Engine; INEI provinces and districts (peru-geojson); HydroBASINS basins with Pfafstetter codes; Meteomatics for an exploratory weather analysis.
  • Languages: Python for harmonization and the backend; JavaScript (React/JSX) for the interface.
  • Processing and storage: pandas, NumPy, DuckDB and Apache Parquet.
  • Backend: FastAPI with OpenAPI documentation, automated HTML reports, pytest (153 tests) and ruff.
  • Frontend and maps: React, Vite and MapLibre GL JS, with Esri World Imagery and OpenFreeMap basemaps; ESLint.
  • Hazard method: Saaty pairwise comparison (the analytic hierarchy process from CENEPRED's manual) for the weights of density, recurrence and most active year.
  • Deployment: Docker, Google Cloud Build and Google Cloud Run (São Paulo region).
  • Collaboration: Git and GitHub with one branch per member, and GitHub Actions to verify the data on every change.
  • Quality testing: independent recomputation scripts, automated browser walkthroughs and load simulation.
  • AI assistance: Claude and Claude Code for the method, code, audits and documentation.
  • Hardware: the team's personal laptops; no special hardware was needed.

How is your project creative?

It treats the sensor change as the central problema, not a technical footnote and anomaly against the local median is more useful to a firefighter tan a raw count, and less sensitive to the sensor. Also it is transparent by design, because exposes the data versión, flags extrapolated months and labels the live layer “not harmonized”, and has a QA role that recomputes the results independently.

Calendar in anomaly mode: each cell shows how far a month was from its own typical value.

What factors did your team consider?

Sensors with different resolution and sensitivity, different confidence scales, the switch from Terra to Terra + Aqua in 2002, posible MODIS drift in 2025 and the day without VIIRS S-NPP. Each factor was validated on held-out years, and the control totals are checked on every change.

For real users, emergency teams, firefighters, land managers and scientists. Hence a simple fire calendar - GeoViewer, accesible colors and clear error messages (empty area, inverted range, no data, area too large).

The "Method and limits" section included in every automated report.
